title: INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING
body:
The course about everything around the code. Every other COMP course hands you a problem
already stated; this one starts a step earlier. How do you find out what to build, how do
you describe it to people who cannot read code, and how do you keep a system changeable
after the original author has left. The recurring theme is [[Complexity]]: software fails at
scale not because any one function is hard but because everything touches everything else,
which is why [[Coupling and Cohesion]] is the most load-bearing idea here.

It formalises the [[Object Oriented Approach]] that [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]
introduced by example and [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] uses in [[Java]].

## Topics

### The discipline

[[Fields in software engineering]] · [[CS]] · [[Information Technology]] ·
[[Projects in software engineering]] · [[Project Success]] · [[Metrics]]

Where software engineering sits relative to [[CS]] and [[Information Technology]], and what
"success" means for a project, which turns out not to be "the code works". [[Metrics]] is
the attempt to measure any of this.

### Process models

[[SDLC]] · [[Models]] · [[Waterfall]] · [[Agile]] · [[software development]] ·
[[Microservices]] · [[YAGNI Principle]]

The [[SDLC]] is the shape of a project: requirements, design, implementation, testing,
maintenance. [[Waterfall]] runs those once, in order, and assumes you got the requirements
right; [[Agile]] runs them repeatedly in small slices and assumes you didn't. The
[[YAGNI Principle]] ("you aren't going to need it") is the practical rule that falls out of
the second assumption.

### Requirements and analysis

[[System analysis]] · [[Software Requirements Analysis]] · [[Problem Recognition]] ·
[[Evaluation and Synthesis]] · [[Modeling]] · [[Specification]] · [[Review]] ·
[[Use Case Diagrams]]

Requirements analysis in five steps: recognise the problem, evaluate and synthesise
alternatives, model it, specify it, review it. [[Use Case Diagrams]] come late in analysis
and earn their place by being readable to non-technical stakeholders, which is the point of
modelling at all.

### Design paradigms

[[Design]] · [[Paradigms]] · [[Structured Approach]] · [[Object Oriented Approach]] ·
[[Complexity]] · [[Coupling and Cohesion]]

Two ways of organising a system. The [[Structured Approach]] decomposes by *function*; the
[[Object Oriented Approach]] decomposes by *thing*, keeping data and the operations on it
together. Either way the target is the same: low coupling between modules, high cohesion
within them.

### Object-oriented analysis and design

[[OOA]] · [[OOD]] · [[OOM]] · [[Object Oriented]] · [[Abstraction]] · [[Object]] ·
[[Classes]] · [[Inheritance]] · [[Polymorphism]] · [[Encapsulation]]

OOA/D/M is the pipeline: analyse the domain into objects, design the classes, model the
result. The claimed benefits are re-usability, reliability ([[Unit testing]]), robustness
([[Exception Handling]]), and extensibility ([[Inheritance]] and [[Polymorphism]]).

### Code quality

[[Code Smells]] · [[Unit testing]] · [[Exception Handling]] · [[Complexity]]

A [[Code Smells|code smell]] is not a bug; it is a surface symptom that the design
underneath has gone wrong. Long methods, duplicated code, and classes that know too much
about each other are all really [[Coupling and Cohesion]] failures.

## Core Facts to Know

- The [[SDLC]] phases are requirements, design, implementation, testing, and maintenance.
- [[Waterfall]] does each phase once, in order, with no going back.
- Waterfall's weakness is that requirements are assumed correct and complete up front.
- [[Agile]] iterates in short cycles and expects the requirements to change.
- The [[YAGNI Principle]] is "you aren't going to need it", so don't build for imagined futures.
- The five steps of [[Software Requirements Analysis]] are problem recognition, evaluation
  and synthesis, modelling, specification, and review.
- [[Use Case Diagrams]] belong to a later stage of analysis and exist to talk to non-technical people.
- **Coupling** is dependence *between* modules; you want it low.
- **Cohesion** is how single-purpose a module is internally; you want it high.
- The [[Structured Approach]] decomposes a system by function.
- The [[Object Oriented Approach]] decomposes a system by object, i.e. data plus behaviour together.
- OOAD is [[OOA]] (analysis), [[OOD]] (design), and [[OOM]] (modelling).
- The four OO pillars are [[Abstraction]], [[Encapsulation]], [[Inheritance]], and [[Polymorphism]].
- [[Inheritance]] and [[Polymorphism]] are what buy extensibility.
- [[Unit testing]] is what buys reliability; [[Exception Handling]] is what buys robustness.
- A [[Code Smells|code smell]] is a symptom of a design problem, not a defect in itself.
- The cost of fixing a defect rises sharply the later in the [[SDLC]] it is found.
- [[Microservices]] trade internal complexity for network and deployment complexity.
- Project success is measured against schedule, budget, and requirements, not just "it runs".

## Related courses

- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]], the same [[Java]] object model from the implementation side:
  [[Inheritance]], [[Polymorphism]], [[Abstract Data Type]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: where [[Object]], [[Classes]],
  [[Class Relationships]], [[Interface]], [[Implementation]], and [[Function design]] are
  first met by example.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]]: [[MVC]], [[REST APIs]], and [[Microservices]] are these
  design principles applied to a real stack.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]], where the error taxonomy matches: [[Compile Errors]], [[Logic Errors]],
  and [[Runtime Errors]] are the same split as [[Assembly Errors]].
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]: [[Complexity]] and [[Coupling and Cohesion]] are exactly why kernels
  are layered the way [[Operating System Structure]] describes.
